title: Cossack Hetmanate
type: vassal and tributary state of the Ottoman Empire

infobox.label: vassal and tributary state of the Ottoman Empire

summary: The Cossack Hetmanate, officially known as the Zaporozhian Host, was a stratocratic state established by Registered [[cossacks|Cossacks]] in Dnieper Ukraine, existing from 1648 to 1764. It played a significant role in [[history-of-ukraine|Ukrainian history]], particularly through its interactions with the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth and the Tsardom of Moscow.

sections.heading: Establishment and Recognition
paragraphs: The Cossack Hetmanate emerged from a major Cossack uprising in the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, led by [[bohdan-khmelnytsky|Bohdan Khmelnytsky]] in 1648. The uprising was fueled by various factors, including corruption, social disenfranchisement, and the growing Cossack population.

The Hetmanate was legally recognized by the Treaty of Zboriv on August 18, 1649, which was signed by Bohdan Khmelnytsky and Adam Kysil, marking a significant outcome of the [[khmelnytsky-uprising|Khmelnytsky Uprising]].

sections.heading: Relations with Moscow
paragraphs: The establishment of vassal relations with the Tsardom of Moscow was formalized in the Treaty of Pereiaslav in 1654, which is regarded as a pivotal moment in the history of the Cossack Hetmanate. However, subsequent agreements, particularly the second Pereiaslav Council in 1659, limited the Hetmanate's independence.

The Treaty of Andrusovo in 1667, conducted without Cossack representation, divided the Hetmanate along the [[dnieper|Dnieper River]], placing the [[zaporizhian-sich|Zaporozhian Sich]] under joint Russian-Polish administration.

sections.heading: Decline and Abolishment
paragraphs: The Hetmanate faced significant challenges following a failed attempt to sever ties with Russia by [[ivan-mazepa|Ivan Mazepa]] in 1708, which led to its incorporation into the Kiev Governorate and restricted autonomy.

Catherine II of Russia officially abolished the position of [[hetman|Hetman]] in 1764, integrating the Cossack Hetmanate into the Little Russia Governorate, with the last remnants of its administrative system dissolved by 1781.

sections.heading: Cultural and Historical Legacy
paragraphs: Despite its eventual disbandment, the Cossack Hetmanate left a lasting legacy, particularly through its ruling class, which played a crucial role in the [[ukrainian-national-revival|Ukrainian national revival]] during the 19th century.

The term '[[ukraine|Ukraine]]' was increasingly used to refer to the lands of the Hetmanate, reflecting a growing sense of national identity among its inhabitants, who were often referred to as the 'Ruthenian nation.'
